Pelagic larvae of the Painted comber from the Cabrera population hatch from fertilised eggs measuring approximately 0.712 millimeters in diameter. The larvae emerge with a modest total length at birth of just 0.13 centimeters [Lb = 0.13 centimeters], a size that coincides with the opening of the mouth and the onset of exogenous feeding. At this developmental stage, the computed wet weight at birth, derived from the egg diameter, is roughly 0.000133 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000133 grams], representing the mass of the newly emerged yolk-sac larva before it begins to rely on planktonic prey. This lecithotrophic phase is brief, as the larvae must quickly encounter suitable food sources to avoid the point of no return. The small initial size places them among the more diminutive teleost larvae in the rocky littoral habitats of the Cabrera Reserve, where they drift as part of the ichthyoplankton community during the late spring and early summer months.

As the juveniles grow and undergo the larval-juvenile transition, they become benthic inhabitants of seagrass meadows and rocky substrates. The average egg dry weight recorded for this population is 0.000010128 grams , a value that reflects the maternal investment in yolk reserves prior to spawning. Field surveys in the Cabrera Reserve have documented that the total length at puberty, marking the point at which mature gonads first appear, is 8.7 centimeters [Lp = 8.7 centimeters]. This measurement corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 6.63 grams [Wwp = 6.63 grams], the body mass of the youngest individual captured with fully developed gonads. The transition from immature juvenile to a reproductively viable organism thus occurs at a relatively modest size compared to other serranids, likely an adaptation to the seasonal productivity of the Mediterranean environment, where early maturation can enhance lifetime reproductive success.

Reproductive timing in this population is closely tied to thermal conditions. The age at first reproduction, which corresponds to the first successful spawning event, has been estimated at 365 days after hatching [tR = estimated at 365 days after hatching] when individuals develop at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This one-year timeframe indicates that most fish are capable of breeding by the end of their first full growing season. The timing of sexual maturation is accelerated by the warm summer temperatures in the reserve, which promote rapid somatic growth and gonadal recrudescence. In contrast, the maximum lifespan, representing the oldest individual ever recorded with mature gonads in the study area, reaches approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days] under an average ambient temperature of 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C]. This longevity, exceeding eleven years, is notable for a fish of this body size and suggests that the Cabrera population enjoys relatively low natural mortality, possibly due to the protective status of the marine reserve.

The ultimate total length attainable by this species, based on the maximum standard length reported in the literature, is 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters]. However, field measurements within the Cabrera Reserve during the month of June have not exceeded 22.5 centimeters, suggesting that local ecological conditions or fishing pressure may constrain the maximum size actually achieved on the grounds. Growth appears to slow considerably after the onset of sexual maturity, with most energy thereafter directed toward repeated spawning events rather than somatic expansion. The iteroparous strategy of the Painted comber is reflected in its reproductive anatomy; histological examination of the gonads reveals asynchronous oocyte development, allowing for multiple spawning bouts within a single season. This reproductive flexibility is advantageous in the variable Mediterranean environment, where prey availability for larvae can be patchy and unpredictable.

Comparative life-history analysis with other serranid species from the northwestern Mediterranean reveals that the Cabrera population of Serranus scriba exhibits an intermediate pace of life. Its lifespan of 4015 days [am = 4015 days] at 18.5 °C [T = 18.5 °C] places it between the shorter-lived Serranus cabrilla and the more long-lived Epinephelus marginatus. The relatively early first reproduction at 365 days [tR = 365 days] after hatching when reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] represents a strategy that balances current reproductive output against future survival. The small birth size of 0.13 centimeters [Lb = 0.13 centimeters] and correspondingly low wet weight at birth of 0.000133 grams [Wwb = 0.000133 grams] are typical of pelagic spawners that produce numerous small offspring. These traits collectively position the Painted comber as a resilient species capable of sustaining viable populations within the protected confines of the Cabrera Archipelago, where ongoing monitoring continues to refine our understanding of its demographic parameters.
